title: Bradycardia and syncope as sole manifestations of a cranial lesion: a case report
case_prompt:
A 69-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with a year-long history of episodic lightheadedness. He described a sensation beginning in his feet, spreading upward, and then feeling lightheaded, hot, and clammy; each episode lasted a few minutes, occurred randomly without identifiable triggers, and was not associated with focal neurologic symptoms. He also reported general malaise over the past year, including fatigue, weakness, and reduced appetite without weight loss.

His medical history was significant only for hypertension, treated with ramipril. He had previously undergone evaluation for ischemic heart disease; an exercise‐tolerance test was negative for ischemic changes, and echocardiography demonstrated good global systolic and diastolic function. Outpatient monitoring with a 7‐day ECG recording showed sinus rhythm with 12 episodes of bradycardia in 24 hours (lowest rate, 23 bpm), ventricular ectopic beats, and pauses in cardiac activity of up to 2.5 seconds; these events occurred at random times, with no ischemic changes, and were not further investigated.

He was a nonsmoker, a social drinker, and lived independently. On examination, temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 170/100 mm Hg, pulse 54 bpm, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, and there was no chest pain.

Initial investigations included normal full blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serum calcium. Lying and standing blood pressures were 170/100 and 160/100 mm Hg, respectively, with a heart rate of 54 bpm and no orthostatic changes. Urinalysis and chest radiograph were normal.

A 12‐lead ECG on admission showed sinus bradycardia at 54 bpm with occasional premature ventricular complexes and no features of an acute ischemic event.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Vasovagal syncope was considered less likely because the episodes occurred spontaneously without identifiable triggers — “The episodes occurred randomly in the past year, were not provoked by any stimuli.”  
2. Orthostatic hypotension was excluded as the patient had similar lying and standing blood pressures with no heart rate change — “Lying and standing blood pressures were 170/100 and 160/100, respectively. His heart rate was 54 bpm without orthostatic changes.”  
3. Infectious causes were excluded by normal urine analysis and chest imaging — “Urine analysis and chest X-ray were normal, ruling out significant infection.”  
4. Metabolic derangements were excluded since routine blood tests were within normal limits — “His blood tests were normal (Table 1), venous blood test was normal (not shown).”  
5. Acute ischemic heart disease was ruled out by ECG showing no ischemic features — “ECG … no features of acute ischemic event.”  
6. Structural cardiac disease was excluded because echocardiography demonstrated normal systolic and diastolic function — “His echocardiogram showed good global systolic and diastolic function.”  
7. Sick sinus syndrome (idiopathic bradycardia) was considered given documented bradycardia and pauses, but the pauses occurred sporadically and were not correlated with symptoms — “7-day electrocardiogram … showed … pauses in cardiac activity < 2.5 seconds … These pauses occurred at random times and were not related to any physical activity or time of day.”  
8. Central nervous system causes were contemplated as a remaining category after exclusion of other etiologies — “Cranial causes for syncope include epilepsy, cerebrovascular accident (CVA), transient ischemic attack (TIA), space-occupying lesion, raised intracranial pressure, and trauma.”
